findings.title: prisma is used but never imported in salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: The new code in getClient() calls `await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })`, but this file has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (the import block at the top only imports jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). This is a `Cannot find name 'prisma'` type-check failure / ReferenceError at runtime, so the build breaks and the Salesforce integration cannot work at all.

findings.title: Credential-sync refresh path returns a raw fetch Response, but the code reads res.data and crashes
findings.body: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` Response from the sync endpoint, which has no `.data` property and whose body is never parsed. The normal path returns GaxiosResponse (`fetchTokens.res`) which does have `.data`. So in the sync path `const token = res?.data` is `undefined` and `googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block treats it as a non-'invalid_grant' error and silently returns myGoogleAuth with the old, expired credentials, so every Google Calendar API call for synced users fails with 401s and the credential is never marked invalid.

findings.title: Sync-path Response object is persisted as the HubSpot credential key, destroying the stored credential
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when credential sync is enabled, but the result is typed/used as `HubspotToken`. In the sync path: `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined so `expiryDate` becomes NaN, `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken)` sets undefined, and `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: hubspotRefreshToken as any } })` JSON-serializes a Response object — i.e. the stored credential key is overwritten with `{"expiryDate": null}`. The user's HubSpot credential (including the refresh token) is permanently wiped and they must reconnect the app.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens is called with credentialId instead of userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)` is invoked as `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)`. The third parameter is sent to the self-hoster's sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`, so the platform receives a credential row id instead of the Cal.com user id. Since credential ids and user ids overlap numerically, the platform can resolve this to a *different* user and return that user's third-party tokens, which would then be stored on this user's credential — a cross-user token leak. Every other app in this PR passes `credential.userId`.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema drops expiry and refresh_token — computed keys collapse and zod strips unknown fields
findings.body: The schema uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`; both evaluate to "[object Object]", so the second overwrites the first, and the schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. Because zod strips unknown keys by default, parsing any token response returns only `{ access_token }` — the comments claiming "any property with a number is the expiry" are wrong. Consequences in the sync path: in zoomvideo `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` becomes NaN (which then fails zoomTokenSchema's z.number() on the next read, breaking Zoom entirely), and office365calendar never updates its stored expiry.

findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token = "refresh_token" overwrites real refresh tokens in the database
findings.body: When a refresh response omits `refresh_token`, the code writes the literal string "refresh_token" into the result. office365calendar then merges this over the stored credential (`{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`) and zoomvideo assigns `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` directly, and both persist it. If the sync feature is later disabled, or a provider omits refresh_token in a normal refresh, the credential's real refresh token is permanently replaced with the placeholder and all future refreshes fail with invalid_grant, requiring the user to reconnect.

findings.title: Zoom refresh passes app slug "zoomvideo" instead of "zoom"
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the self-hoster's sync endpoint, but Zoom's app slug everywhere else is "zoom" (see zoomvideo/api/callback.ts which stores `appId: "zoom"`, and the new webhook endpoint which looks up `prisma.app` by slug). The platform cannot resolve "zoomvideo" to the Zoom app, so token refresh via the sync endpoint will fail for Zoom. Every other app passes its real slug ("google-calendar", "msteams", "webex", etc.).

findings.title: axios response shape assumed, but sync path returns a fetch Response
findings.body: The normal refresh function returns an AxiosResponse (read via `tokenInfo.data`), but `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` when sync is enabled, which has no `.data`. `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)` then throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`, so Zoho Bigin token refresh always crashes when credential sync is enabled. The same class of mismatch applies to zohocrm.

findings.title: axios/fetch response mismatch breaks ZohoCRM refresh when sync is enabled
findings.body: The wrapped refresh function returns an AxiosResponse, but the sync branch of `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw fetch `Response` with no `.data` property. `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` therefore throws a TypeError; it is swallowed by `catch (e) { this.log.error(e); }`, leaving `this.accessToken` unset/stale. All subsequent Zoho CRM API calls go out with an empty or expired `Zoho-oauthtoken` header and fail, silently breaking the integration for synced users.

findings.title: Webex refresh always rejects when credential sync is enabled
findings.body: Unlike the other apps, webex kept validating with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse(responseBody)`, which requires `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`, and literal `scope`/`token_type` values. The documented sync-endpoint contract ("response should only contain the access token and expiry date") can never satisfy this schema, so `parsedToken.success` is always false and refresh always rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — Webex is broken whenever credential sync is on.

findings.title: Lark refresh expects Lark's {code, data} envelope but sync endpoint returns a flat minimal payload
findings.body: The sync-path response from `refreshOAuthTokens` is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>` and then read as `data.data.refresh_token`, `data.data.refresh_expires_in`, etc. The sync endpoint returns a flat `{access_token, expiry}` payload (per the documented contract in refreshOAuthTokens), so `data.data` is undefined and the refresh throws (or stores undefined token fields into the credential key). Lark calendar refresh is broken when credential sync is enabled.

findings.title: Salesforce refresh runs on every service instantiation and the connection is built with the stale access token
findings.body: getClient() now performs a refresh-token exchange with Salesforce every time a CalendarService is constructed, even when the stored access token is still valid — adding a blocking network round trip (and Salesforce token-endpoint rate-limit exposure) to every calendar operation, and overwriting the DB key each time, which also fights the webhook's source-of-truth model when sync is enabled. Additionally, after refreshing and persisting the new token, the jsforce.Connection is created with the OLD `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` instead of `accessTokenParsed.data`, so the fresh token is never actually used.

findings.title: Invalid webhook payloads throw unhandled 500s instead of 4xx responses
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on any malformed body, and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...))` (line 57) throws on a wrongly encrypted or non-JSON payload; neither is wrapped in try/catch, so callers get an unhandled 500 with a stack trace rather than a 400. The handler also never checks `req.method`, so even a GET with no body hits these throwing paths. The webhook secret comparison at line 25 is also not constant-time.

findings.title: findFirst by userId+appId can overwrite the wrong credential for multi-account apps
findings.body: Cal.com allows a user to connect multiple accounts for the same app (e.g. several Google or Office 365 calendars), producing multiple Credential rows with the same userId and appId. The webhook's `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks an arbitrary one and overwrites its key with the pushed credentials, so the platform can silently clobber the tokens of a different account than intended. The payload needs an account identifier (e.g. email/external id) to target the correct credential.

findings.title: Outbound request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication
findings.body: The POST to the self-hoster's sync endpoint sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body — no shared secret, signature, or header (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is only checked on the inbound webhook). The platform endpoint therefore cannot verify the request genuinely comes from its Cal.com instance; anyone who can reach that endpoint can request freshly refreshed third-party OAuth tokens for any user id / app. The implementation should include the shared secret (or an HMAC) so the platform can authenticate the caller.

findings.title: No tests for the webhook endpoint or the sync refresh paths
findings.body: The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. This change adds a new authenticated credential-writing endpoint and rewires token refresh for nine integrations with two divergent code paths (direct provider refresh vs. platform sync endpoint); the response-shape mismatches introduced here (axios vs fetch, GaxiosResponse vs fetch Response) are exactly the kind of regression a small unit/integration test per service would have caught.
